affected: Clearview AI — USD 50M settlement; Illinois residents whose biometric data was collected without consent; law enforcement agencies using biased outputs
Clearview AI; individuals whose biometric data was scraped (nationwide BIPA settlement class)
description: Clearview AI reached a settlement in a class action lawsuit over its facial recognition system's biometric data collection and demonstrated racial bias. The lawsuit, filed under Illinois BIPA (Biometric Information Privacy Act), alleged that Clearview scraped billions of facial images from the internet without consent and that the resulting system exhibited measurable accuracy disparities across racial groups. The settlement established a USD 50 million fund and required Clearview to implement bias testing, obtain consent for US data collection, and submit to third-party audits. The case established legal precedent that AI training data bias creates direct financial liability.

Class members in consolidated Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) litigation against Clearview AI, a facial recognition company that built a database of more than 60 billion facial images by scraping photographs from the internet, reached a settlement that U.S. District Judge Sharon Johnson Coleman approved on 2025-03-20. Unusually, the settlement gives the class a 23% equity stake in Clearview rather than a cash fund; commentary values the stake at approximately $51.75 million as of January 2024, with payment triggered by events such as an IPO or a liquidation event. State attorneys general objected to the settlement.
impact: USD 50M settlement establishes financial precedent for AI training data bias; BIPA violations for unconsented biometric collection; mandatory bias testing + third-party audits as structural remedy; precedent for other states and jurisdictions

BIPA class settlement paid as a 23% equity stake in Clearview AI for people whose facial images were collected without consent; first-of-its-kind equity-based resolution of biometric privacy litigation

affected: OpenAI / ChatGPT — EUR 15M fine; all LLM providers operating in EU face precedent; structural remedies required
OpenAI / ChatGPT (Italy; case referred to the Irish DPC as lead supervisory authority)
description: The Italian Data Protection Authority (Garante per la protezione dei dati personali) issued its final enforcement decision against OpenAI regarding ChatGPT's compliance with GDPR. Following the initial March 2023 suspension and subsequent investigation, the Garante found violations of Articles 5 (data minimization), 6 (lawfulness — insufficient legal basis for training data processing), 13 (transparency — inadequate privacy notice), and 25 (data protection by design). The decision imposed a EUR 15 million fine and required structural remedies including age verification, opt-out mechanisms for training data, and enhanced transparency about data processing. This is the first major GDPR enforcement action specifically targeting an LLM provider's training data practices.

On 2024-12-20 the Italian data protection authority (Garante per la protezione dei dati personali) announced that it had closed its investigation of OpenAI's ChatGPT service, opened in March 2023, with a corrective and sanctioning decision and a fine of EUR 15 million, calculated also taking into account the company's cooperative attitude. The Garante found that OpenAI had not notified it of the data breach suffered in March 2023, had processed users' personal data to train ChatGPT without first identifying an adequate legal basis, had breached the principle of transparency and the related information obligations, and had provided no age-verification mechanism, exposing children under 13 to responses inappropriate to their development. It ordered OpenAI to run a six-month institutional communication campaign on radio, television, newspapers and the internet, and passed the case file to the Irish DPC as lead supervisory authority. The Garante's page now notes that decision No. 755 of 2 November 2024 was temporarily removed from its website after judgment No. 4153/2026 of the Tribunal of Rome (published 2026-03-18) upheld OpenAI's opposition to it.
impact: First major GDPR enforcement targeting LLM training data; establishes precedent that AI training on personal data requires explicit legal basis; EUR 15M fine; structural remedies (age verification, opt-out, transparency) now expected industry-wide

affected: Microsoft Copilot Studio — enterprise agents with business data access
Microsoft Copilot Studio agents with knowledge sources and customer-data tools
description: Agents built in Microsoft Copilot Studio were public by default and lacked authentication. Attackers could enumerate and access exposed agents, pulling confidential business data from production environments.

Zenity Labs researchers reported that Microsoft Copilot Studio agents were vulnerable to prompt injection via triggers (reported to MSRC on 2025-02-21; Microsoft confirmed the behaviour on 2025-03-13 and issued a fix on 2025-04-24). In a two-part write-up (2025-06-11 discovery phase, 2025-07-07 exfiltration phase) they showed how an attacker could discover a customer-service agent's knowledge sources and tools and then use prompt injection ("AIjacking") to exfiltrate the agent's knowledge-source data, about 100 rows of data in a single iteration, and customer records reachable through the agent's connected tools.
impact: Unauthorized agent access; business intelligence theft; data exfiltration

affected: OpenAI o1, o1-mini, o3-mini reasoning models — attack class is specific to CoT reasoning models; applicable to any model with extended reasoning capabilities
Large reasoning models evaluated by the authors: OpenAI o1/o3, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking
description: Multiple researchers independently demonstrated that OpenAI's o1 and o3 reasoning models — which use extended chain-of-thought (CoT) processing — are susceptible to jailbreaks that exploit the reasoning chain itself. By embedding adversarial instructions that interact with the model's internal reasoning steps, attackers can cause the model to "reason its way" into compliance with harmful requests. The attack exploits the fact that safety training operates on the final output but the CoT steps can establish logical premises that make harmful conclusions appear well-reasoned. OpenAI acknowledged the attack class and noted that reasoning models present novel safety challenges distinct from standard instruction-following models.

Researchers introduced H-CoT (Hijacking Chain-of-Thought), a jailbreak that leverages a model's own displayed intermediate reasoning to jailbreak its chain-of-thought safety reasoning mechanism, together with the Malicious-Educator benchmark, which disguises extremely dangerous or malicious requests beneath seemingly legitimate educational prompts. They report severe security flaws in commercial large reasoning models including OpenAI o1/o3, DeepSeek-R1 and Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking: OpenAI's o1 initially maintained a refusal rate of about 98%, subsequent model updates significantly compromised its safety, and under H-CoT refusal rates dropped from 98% to below 2%.
impact: Novel jailbreak class specific to reasoning models; safety training on final output is insufficient when CoT steps can establish adversarial premises; challenges the assumption that more capable reasoning improves safety
Under H-CoT the refusal rate of OpenAI o1 dropped from about 98% to below 2% (authors' report); displaying the safety reasoning makes it available for hijacking

affected: Job candidates — particularly women applying for technical roles
Job candidates, particularly women applying through automated CV screening
description: Continued reporting revealed that multiple enterprise AI recruiting tools, following the pattern first reported with Amazon's internal tool, systematically downranked female candidates. Analysis showed the models learned historical hiring biases from training data where male candidates were disproportionately hired for technical roles. The EEOC issued formal guidance that AI-driven hiring discrimination violates Title VII regardless of whether bias was intentional. Several vendors settled with affected candidates.

In 2018 Reuters reported, and the BBC summarized on 2018-10-10, that Amazon had scrapped an experimental machine-learning recruitment tool that scored candidates from one to five stars: by 2015 it was clear the system was not rating candidates in a gender-neutral way because it was built on CVs submitted to the firm mostly by men, and it penalised CVs that included the word "women"; the program was edited to be neutral to the term but could not be relied on, and the project was abandoned. On 2023-05-18 the US EEOC released technical assistance on assessing adverse impact in software, algorithms and AI used in employment selection procedures under Title VII, stating that an employer can be held responsible for an algorithmic selection procedure that has an adverse impact even if the tool is designed or administered by a software vendor.
impact: EEOC enforcement guidance; vendor settlements; regulatory precedent for AI hiring discrimination; legislative proposals
Gender bias in an automated hiring tool led to its abandonment; EEOC technical assistance (May 2023) on disparate impact of algorithmic selection tools

affected: Endpoint detection platforms — traditional signature and behavioural detection methods
Endpoint detection and response products (one unidentified "industry leading" EDR tested)
description: Security researchers demonstrated that LLMs could generate polymorphic malware variants that evade traditional signature-based and behavioural endpoint detection. By iteratively prompting the model to rewrite malware code with different obfuscation techniques, API call patterns, and control flow while maintaining functionality, the generated variants bypassed detection by major EDR platforms including CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, and Microsoft Defender.

Researchers from HYAS Labs demonstrated BlackMamba, a proof-of-concept attack that uses a large language model (the technology behind ChatGPT) to synthesize polymorphic keylogger functionality on the fly. The attack is "truly polymorphic" because it resynthesizes its keylogging capability every time it executes, and it works without command-and-control infrastructure. HYAS reported testing it against an EDR system that was not identified but was characterized as "industry leading", often resulting in zero alerts or detections. Captured data such as usernames, passwords and credit card numbers was sent out through a malicious Microsoft Teams channel. Reported in March 2023.
impact: Fundamental challenge to signature-based detection; arms race between AI-generated attacks and AI-assisted defence
A proof-of-concept LLM-synthesized polymorphic keylogger evaded an unnamed EDR product in the researchers' tests (often zero alerts), challenging signature and behavioral detection

affected: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3, Mistral Large, and 3 others — all tested via standard chat-completion API; attack is model-agnostic
13 state-of-the-art LLMs evaluated in the paper (the abstract does not enumerate them)
description: Researchers from UCSB demonstrated MathPrompt — a jailbreak technique that encodes harmful prompts into symbolic mathematics (set theory notation, abstract algebra, graph theory) before submitting to LLMs. The technique exploits the fact that LLMs have strong mathematical reasoning capabilities but safety training is almost entirely focused on natural language. Harmful requests encoded as mathematical problems bypass content filters with 73.6% success rate across 8 frontier models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini 1.5, Llama 3, Mistral, etc.). The attack requires no special access — it uses the standard chat API. This is a direct instance of the Encoding category (E-class) in the LAAF technique taxonomy.

MathPrompt is a jailbreaking technique that encodes harmful natural-language prompts into mathematical problems, exploiting LLMs' capabilities in symbolic mathematics to bypass their safety mechanisms. Across 13 state-of-the-art LLMs the authors report an average attack success rate of 73.6%, and an analysis of embedding vectors shows a substantial semantic shift between original and encoded prompts, which helps explain the attack's success. The authors conclude that existing safety training mechanisms do not generalize to mathematically encoded inputs.
impact: 73.6% harmful content bypass rate across frontier models; demonstrates a systematic gap between mathematical reasoning capability and safety alignment coverage; attack is trivially automatable and requires no special access
Average attack success rate of 73.6% across 13 LLMs as reported by the authors; indicates a gap between mathematical-reasoning capability and safety-training coverage

affected: Scale AI, Sama, and AI data labeling companies globally; downstream: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta (any company using third-party RLHF or annotation services); annotation workers in Kenya, India, Philippines
Sama content moderators and data labelers in Nairobi, Kenya working on OpenAI's account
description: Investigations by TIME and The Guardian revealed systematic privacy violations in AI data labeling supply chains. Workers at Sama (previously contracted by OpenAI for RLHF content moderation labeling) and similar data annotation companies in Kenya, India, and the Philippines were exposed to traumatic content (violence, CSAM, hate speech) without adequate psychological support, earning as little as $1.32/hour. Additionally, the annotation platforms used by these workers often lacked basic data security — labeled data containing personal information (medical records, legal documents, private communications) was accessible to workers without need-to-know controls, and annotation task metadata (worker identity, labeling speed, accuracy) was collected without informed consent. The investigation revealed that the third-party AI data supply chain had minimal security governance, creating both worker welfare and data security risks that propagated into the training data of major production models.

TIME and The Guardian reported on the working conditions of data labelers and content moderators employed by Sama, a California-headquartered data annotation company, on OpenAI's behalf in Nairobi, Kenya. TIME (2023-01-18) reported that Sama data labelers were paid a take-home wage of between around $1.32 and $2 per hour, depending on seniority and performance. The Guardian (2023-08-02) reported that the 51 moderators in Nairobi working on Sama's OpenAI account reviewed texts, and some images, depicting graphic scenes of violence, self-harm, murder, rape, necrophilia and child abuse, and that in a petition they allege psychological trauma, low pay and abrupt dismissal; a Sama spokesperson said workers were paid between $1.46 and $3.74 an hour.
impact: Worker exploitation and traumatic content exposure; personal data from annotation tasks (medical, legal, private) accessible without need-to-know; third-party supply chain as unaudited attack surface for training data; demonstrates that AI data security extends to the entire labeling supply chain

affected: Stability AI / Stable Diffusion — legal action in UK and US; LAION dataset users; all image generation models trained on web-scraped data
LAION-5B and LAION-400M, and models trained on them such as Stable Diffusion
description: Stability AI faced legal action and regulatory scrutiny after researchers demonstrated that Stable Diffusion models could generate child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The Stanford Internet Observatory documented that the LAION-5B training dataset — used to train Stable Diffusion — contained over 3,000 instances of suspected CSAM, which the model learned to reproduce and recombine. Despite content filters, researchers bypassed them using negative prompts, fine-tuning, and model merging techniques. The case established that (1) training data contamination directly creates output safety risks, (2) post-hoc content filters are insufficient when the model has learned harmful patterns, and (3) synthetic CSAM carries the same legal liability as real CSAM in most jurisdictions.

In December 2023 a Stanford Internet Observatory study, reported by 404 Media, found 3,226 suspected instances of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), 1,008 of which were externally validated, in LAION-5B, the machine learning dataset used by Stable Diffusion and other major AI products. LAION took LAION-5B and LAION-400M down temporarily out of an abundance of caution to ensure they were safe before republishing. On 2024-08-30 LAION released Re-LAION-5B, cleaned of known links to suspected CSAM using hash lists from the Internet Watch Foundation and the Canadian Center for Child Protection, in which 2236 links were removed.
impact: Training data contamination → model generates illegal content; post-hoc filters insufficient; synthetic CSAM carries full legal liability; LAION-5B removed and re-released with filtering; precedent for training data liability
Suspected CSAM links found in a web-scale training dataset used for image-generation models; the dataset was withdrawn and later re-released with known links removed

affected: GitHub Copilot users — risk of introducing unlicensed code or live credentials into projects
GitHub Copilot users and the authors of open-source code used to train it
description: Multiple studies showed that GitHub Copilot — trained on public GitHub repositories — would reproduce verbatim code from its training data, including open-source code with restrictive licenses (GPL, etc.) and, more critically, code containing hardcoded API keys, passwords, and private keys that were committed to public repositories. Researchers at NYU demonstrated that Copilot suggestions included identifiable code from training data ~1% of the time for common patterns, and that secrets appeared in a measurable fraction of generated code. This led to the Doe v. GitHub class action lawsuit.

GitHub Copilot, GitHub's AI coding assistant unveiled in June 2021, is trained on public code repositories, many of them published with open-source licenses. A proposed class action lawsuit against Microsoft, GitHub and OpenAI (reported by The Verge on 2022-11-08) alleges that the creation of Copilot relies on "software piracy on an unprecedented scale"; the key question in the lawsuit is whether open-source code can be reproduced by AI without attached licenses.
impact: License compliance violations; potential exposure of live API keys from training data; class action lawsuit filed
License compliance questions over open-source code reproduced by an AI coding assistant; proposed class action lawsuit filed

affected: TikTok / ByteDance — EUR 345M fine + EUR 12B data localization investment; all AI companies processing EU personal data with non-EU infrastructure
TikTok / ByteDance; users aged 13 to 17 whose accounts were public by default in 2020
description: The Irish Data Protection Commission fined TikTok EUR 345 million for GDPR violations related to children's data processing and transparency failures. Separately, ongoing EU regulatory pressure over TikTok's data transfers to China led to the mandatory implementation of Project Clover — a EUR 12 billion program to localize European user data in European data centers. While not AI-specific, the case directly impacts TikTok's recommendation algorithm (an AI system) because training data, user interaction data, and model inference data must now be processed within EU borders. The enforcement established that AI systems processing EU personal data must comply with data localization requirements, and that the AI recommendation engine cannot be separated from the data governance obligations. This is the defining case for DSGAI20 — data localization violations in AI systems.

On 2023-09-15 Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined TikTok EUR 345 million under the GDPR for how the app handled children's data in 2020, particularly around age verification and privacy settings. The DPC found that TikTok had not been transparent enough with children about its privacy settings and that accounts made by users aged 13 to 17 were public by default on registration, which the Data Protection Commissioner said infringed the GDPR's data-protection-by-design-and-by-default requirements. TikTok was given three months to bring its data processing into compliance and said it respectfully disagreed with the decision, particularly the level of the fine.
impact: EUR 345M fine; EUR 12B infrastructure investment for data localization; establishes that AI recommendation systems cannot bypass data localization requirements; precedent for all AI companies with cross-border data flows
EUR 345 million GDPR fine, at the time the biggest TikTok had received from regulators; three months to bring data processing into compliance
